Today's profile, a policy that did the opposite of what its designers intended.
In the summer of 2003, as the first phase of reservoir filling behind the three gorgeous
dam raised water levels more than 100 meters along the Yang Sea, residents near the town
of Wushan watched entire hillsides begin to move.
What made that rise so consequential was the sheer speed at which the water was added.
The reservoir did not fill gradually over decades, but instead climbed more than 100 meters
in a single season, placing an entirely new load on slopes that had never carried it before.
People living on those slopes noticed the ground shifting under fields they had worked for generations.
And the movement was not limited to one hillside, but appeared across multiple locations at
roughly the same time the water reached its new elevation.
Cracks opened in fields that had been farmed for generations, and small slides sent mud and
rock into the rising water.
Those cracks were not random surface fishers, they formed where the added saturation reduced
the friction that had previously held soil and rock in place, allowing gravity to pull
material downslope once the water table rose.
The small slides that followed carried loose debris directly into the reservoir, showing
how quickly the change in moisture could turn stable ground into something that behaved like
a fluid.
The structure had been built to tame floods and generate electricity on a scale never attempted
before.
Instead, the weight of the water itself started reshaping the surrounding geology.
The original calculations had treated the reservoir as a static body of water whose primary
effects would be downstream.
Yet the mass itself, once impounded, began to press on the underlying rock in ways that
altered local stress fields almost immediately.
The idea of a massive dam at the Three Gorges site dates to Sunyat Sen's 1919 proposal
to improve navigation and irrigation on the Yang Sea.
That early vision already recognized the river's dual character as both a lifeline and a recurring
threat.
And later planners kept returning to the same narrow stretch of valley because the topography
offered a natural constriction where a single barrier could influence hundreds of kilometers
of river.
Chinese leaders revisited the concept after devastating floods in 1954 that killed more than
30,000 people and displaced millions.
Those floods demonstrated that existing levees and smaller reservoirs could not contain the
volume of water that arrived during an extreme monsoon.
So the memory of that single year kept the larger project alive in official planning documents
for decades afterward.
By the 1980s, rapid economic growth created urgent demand for electricity and greater protection
for the densely populated middle and lower Yang Sea basin.
Industrial output was expanding at double-digit rates in coastal provinces and planners calculated
that the gap between supply and demand would widen unless a single large source could
be added.
At the same time, the growing cities and farmland downstream needed assurance that another
1954 scale flood would not erase years of investment.
Premier Li Peng, a hydraulic engineer by training, championed the project as essential infrastructure
that would both prevent catastrophe and supply roughly one-tenth of the country's power
needs at the time.
Because he understood the arithmetic of reservoir storage and turbine output, he could argue
that one structure could deliver both flood space volume and generating capacity without requiring
separate investments in multiple smaller dams.
The National People's Congress formally approved construction in 1992 after years of feasibility
studies that emphasized flood storage capacity of 22 billion cubic meters and a generating capacity
of 22,500 megawatts.
Those studies framed the numbers as complementary rather than competing.
The same volume held back during peak flow could later be released through turbines, turning
a safety margin into an energy asset measured in thousands of megawatts.
At the scale envisioned, the dam appeared to offer a single intervention capable of addressing
multiple national priorities simultaneously.
The arithmetic suggested that one concrete structure, one reservoir and one set of turbines
could reduce flood peaks, generate electricity, and improve navigation all at once, which
made the project attractive when budgets and political attention were finite.
Construction began in 1994 at Sandoping in Hubei Province.
The site was chosen because the valley narrows there, allowing the dam to be anchored into
bedrock on both banks while the reservoir extended upstream for roughly 660 kilometers once complete.
The reservoir was filled in stages, reaching 135 meters in 2003, 156 meters in 2006, and
the final operating level of 175 meters in 2010.
Each increment added hundreds of millions of cubic meters of water and the staged approach
was intended to let engineers observe how the slopes and faults responded before committing
the full load.
Official reports at the time highlighted successful power generation that began feeding the grid
in 2003, and the relocation of roughly 1.13 million residents from 13 cities and hundreds
of villages.
The relocation itself required building new towns on higher ground, new roads, and new farmland
all completed on a timetable that matched the rising water levels.
Proponents cited reduced flood peaks downstream during the 2010 and 2012 monsoon seasons as early
validation.
Those seasons brought rainfall totals comparable to earlier flood years, yet the measured
crest heights below the dam were lower by several meters, which appeared to confirm that the
storage volume was performing as modeled.
Some geologists and environmental researchers inside and outside China had warned during
the approval process that the unprecedented water load could affect seismic activity and
slope stability, yet the project moved forward with monitoring programs intended to manage
those risks.
The monitoring networks were designed to detect movement after it began rather than to
predict exactly where or when a slope would fail under the new saturation conditions.
Once the reservoir reached full capacity, the added weight of approximately 39 billion tons
of water altered stresses on the crust beneath the 660 kilometer reservoir.
39 billion tons is roughly the mass of a 40 meter thick layer spread across the entire
reservoir surface, and that layer pressed downward on rock that had previously supported only air
and soil, changing the balance of forces along existing faults.
seismic stations recorded a measurable increase in small earthquakes, particularly along the
Zigui and Badong segments of the Yang Sea, with events clustered after rapid water level rises.
The timing suggested that the added poor pressure in the rock reduced the effective normal
stress on fault planes, allowing small slips to occur sooner than they would have under natural
rainfall alone.
On the reservoir margins, saturation of previously dry slopes triggered hundreds of landslides.
The 2003 Ken Zhang Ping slide killed 24 people and blocked a tributary.
That slide occurred when water rapidly entered joints and fractures that had stayed dry for
centuries, turning what had been a stable hillside into a mass that slid as a single unit
into the reservoir.
Further downstream, the dam trapped most of the Yang Sea's sediment load, starving the river
channel and coastal delta of material needed to maintain elevation against subsidence and sea level
rise. Without the yearly replenishment of silt, the riverbed downstream began to erode,
and the delta front lost the sediment that had previously offset gradual sinking of the land surface.
Towns in farmland that had been relocated to higher ground sometimes found themselves on
slopes newly prone to failure because the relocated communities themselves altered drainage patterns.
New roads and house foundations changed how rainwater flowed across those slopes, concentrating water
in places that had not been designed to carry it, which in turn raised local groundwater levels
and reduced slope stability further. The combination of these effects induced seismicity,
repeated landslides and sediment starvation arose directly from the decision to impound such
an enormous volume of water in a tectonically active, steeply incised valley. Each individual
process had been discussed in the feasibility studies, yet the studies treated them as separate
monitoring tasks, rather than as coupled consequences that could reinforce one another once the reservoir
was full. Chinese authorities expanded monitoring networks and imposed seasonal water level restrictions
to reduce landslide risk during the monsoon. The restrictions meant drawing the reservoir down by
several meters before the heaviest rains arrived, which lowered the saturation level on the most vulnerable
slopes even though it also reduced the amount of water available for power generation at that moment.
Some of the most unstable slopes received engineered stabilization, yet new slides continued to appear
after heavy rains or rapid drawdowns. The stabilization measures, such as drainage tunnels and
retaining structures, address the slopes that had already shown movement, but they could not
eliminate the underlying change in groundwater conditions created by the reservoir's presence.
The sediment deficit has required periodic flushing operations that temporarily lower reservoir
levels, trading power generation and flood storage for downstream channel maintenance.
During flushing, operators open the gates to let sediment laden water pass through,
which restores some material to the lower river, but also means the reservoir cannot hold its
full flood control volume or run its turbines at full capacity for those days or weeks.
No reversal of the dam itself has been contemplated. Instead, the operating regime has been adjusted
iteratively. Each adjustment is tested against the latest monitoring data and the operating rules
are revised again when new slides appear or when downstream erosion measurements exceed earlier
thresholds. Today, the structure still supplies roughly 100 terawatt hours annually while providing
measurable flood peak reduction, even as geological management remains an ongoing operational cost.
The energy figure represents a large fraction of the original design output, yet the additional
expense of slope monitoring, flushing, and stabilization was not part of the 1992 cost estimates.
Interventions that concentrate enormous mass or force in one location can shift stresses
throughout surrounding physical systems in ways that are difficult to model completely beforehand.
When the mass in question is on the order of tens of billions of tons of water,
even small changes in poor pressure or sediment supply can propagate through the landscape faster
than the original models anticipated. When the scale of a project approaches the magnitude
of natural geological forces, second order effects on slopes, faults, and sediment transport become
first order concerns rather than minor externalities. The distinction matters because the same volume of
water that delivers flood protection and electricity also changes the boundary conditions for every
slope and fault within the reservoirs reach. Decision makers facing similarly large proposals today
can usefully ask what existing stresses in the landscape or society will be amplified,
not merely whether the primary objective will be met. The question shifts attention from the
intended benefit to the pre-existing conditions that the new load will interact with, whether those
conditions are faults, sediment budgets, or drainage patterns on relocated land.
How might we test the stability of an entire system before committing to changes whose physical
consequences cannot be undone? One approach is to introduce the load in smaller increments while
maintaining independent observation networks that can halt or reverse the next increment if measured
responses exceed earlier projections. And that's where today's story leaves us. If it changed how you
